## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\begin{marginfigure}
\resizebox{0.92\linewidth}{!}{\mlphysicalstackfull{20}{20}{100}{20}{20}}
\end{marginfigure}
:::

_Why must a physical AI systems engineer master mechanical inertia, winding thermal limits, and power distribution rail droop before writing a single line of motor control policy?_

A mobile manipulator can recognize an obstacle correctly and still strike it if its body cannot stop within the remaining distance. The same machine can hold a payload without moving while its motor windings overheat, or lose its controller when a sudden demand for current pulls the supply voltage too low. These failures arise from limits that prediction accuracy alone cannot reveal. Physical AI engineering requires connecting a proposed action to the motion, heat, and electrical demand it creates, then establishing which limit the assembled machine reaches first. Measurements must also establish the conditions under which those limits hold, because a change in payload, floor surface, cooling, or battery state changes what the machine can deliver. The body's limits therefore govern what the permission path may admit before a command crosses the causal boundary and produces irreversible physical work.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Calculate observation freshness limits from measurement age and the machine's allowable motion
- Calculate stopping distance and the admissible speed ceiling from pre-brake delay, credible deceleration, and clearance overheads
- Evaluate actuator and transmission choices against response limits, reflected inertia, and mechanical impedance
- Estimate sustainable motor duty cycles from heat generation, cooling, and operating conditions
- Budget electrical supply margins for simultaneous actuation, computation, and regenerative braking
- Specify the elements of a limit record that states a measured limit's conditions, uncertainty, margin, runtime detector, and evidence category
- Identify which budget binds first for a given machine and maneuver, and justify isolating the permission path on its own held-up supply

:::

## The Five Physical Budgets {#sec-body-five-budgets}

Every action a learned model proposes ends as current in a motor winding, and from that point the body, not the model, determines what happens. Machine learning practice rarely has to reason about that step. A policy trained in simulation usually meets an idealized plant in which commanded torque appears at once, heat never accumulates, and the supply voltage never moves, and a physical machine honors none of those assumptions. The **physical body**\index{Physical body!definition} is the coupled plant of actuators, transmissions, structural linkages, power electronics, and sensors that turns a command into motion. Its limits constrain even a correctly chosen action. A brake command requires time to build force and distance to dissipate kinetic energy; a holding command draws current and accumulates heat even when the arm does not move.

The proposal boundary in @sec-boundary-machine-model gives the permission path responsibility for admitting action, and the body supplies the limits that make that decision meaningful. Before it admits a command, the permission path must know whether the observation is still useful, whether the machine can stop, whether the drive can deliver the requested motion, whether the winding can tolerate its duration, and whether the electrical supply remains usable. These are the five physical budgets. Their mechanisms connect in that order: delay consumes stopping distance; stopping requires delivered torque; torque generates heat and draws current from the shared supply. The central question is which of these limits the assembled machine reaches first for a given maneuver, and on what evidence. We derive each budget from introductory mechanics and circuits, show how to measure it on the assembled machine and record it with its conditions, and then compare the five to find the one that binds.

1. **Measurement freshness** ($t_{\text{age}}$)\index{Measurement freshness!definition}: The observation must remain useful until the actuator responds. Motion during exposure, transport, computation, and actuation consumes the allowable position error.
2. **Kinetic momentum** ($E_k, p$)\index{Kinetic momentum!definition}: The moving machine carries kinetic energy ($E_k = \frac{1}{2} m v^2$) and momentum ($p = mv$). Stopping requires retarding force over a finite distance, so the chosen speed must leave enough clearance for delay and braking.
3. **Actuator bandwidth and reflected inertia** ($f_a, N^2 J$)\index{Actuator bandwidth!definition}\index{Reflected inertia!definition}: Winding inductance and available voltage limit how quickly torque changes. Gearing increases delivered torque but also increases the rotor inertia that the joint must accelerate, limiting the motion a command can produce.
4. **Thermal capacity** ($T_j$)\index{Thermal capacity!definition}: Current generates heat in the windings and inverter. Cooling limits sustained torque, while stored heat limits the duration and repetition of torque bursts.
5. **Electrical power integrity** ($V_{\text{rail}}$)\index{Electrical power integrity!definition}: Compute and drives draw from a finite shared supply. Simultaneous demand must leave sufficient voltage for control, and braking must leave somewhere for returned energy to go.

Under the **Simultaneous Admission Invariant**, motion permission requires a non-negative margin in every budget before the permission path commits torque to hardware registers. Each margin must be checked in its own units; time, distance, torque, temperature, and voltage are separate constraints, not interchangeable quantities:
$$\begin{aligned}
t_{\text{age}} &\le \Delta t_{\text{fresh}}, \\
d_{\text{stop}} &\le D_{\text{clear}}, \\
|\tau_{\text{cmd}}| &\le \tau_{\text{out, max}}, \\
\hat{T}_{\text{wind}} &\le T_{\text{limit}}, \\
V_{\text{rail, min}} &\ge V_{\text{uvlo}}.
\end{aligned}$$
Here $\tau_{\text{cmd}}$ is requested torque and $\tau_{\text{out, max}}$ is the maximum deliverable output torque under the current conditions. The estimated winding temperature $\hat{T}_{\text{wind}}$ must remain below its limit, while the lowest rail voltage $V_{\text{rail, min}}$ must remain above the undervoltage-lockout threshold $V_{\text{uvlo}}$ at which the supply regulator shuts down. All five inequalities must hold simultaneously. A surplus in four budgets cannot compensate for a deficit in the fifth: a fresh observation cannot prevent a stop from overrunning if kinetic energy exceeds available clearance, and abundant battery energy cannot prevent an actuator from burning out if thermal dissipation limits are violated.

::: {.callout-perspective title="Why physical limits bound physical AI architecture"}
The permission path needs limits on delivered physical behavior. An accepted torque request does not establish that the drive can produce it, and removing electrical power does not establish that the machine will stop within clearance. The five budgets connect software requests to measurable response under declared operating conditions.
:::

```{python}
#| label: body-machine-momentum-calc
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE RUNNING MACHINE'S MOMENTUM (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: the running-machine sentence in @sec-body-five-budgets.
# │ Goal:    Give the warehouse mobile manipulator's kinetic energy at its
# │          drive limit with the tote rack loaded.
# │ Show:    368 kg (upper bound) at 1.5 m/s carries 414 J.
# │ How:     calc_kinetic_energy on RM.loaded_mass and RM.base.max_velocity.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_mass, fmt_velocity, fmt_energy, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class MachineMomentum:
    """Kinetic energy of the loaded running machine at its drive limit."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    m_loaded = RM.loaded_mass  # category: derived (upper bound, full tote rack)
    v_drive = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative (drive limit)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    e_k = calc_kinetic_energy(m_loaded, v_drive).to(joule)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(m_loaded.to(kilogram).magnitude - 368.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected loaded mass: {m_loaded}")
    check(abs(e_k.magnitude - 414.0) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected kinetic energy: {e_k}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    m_loaded_str = fmt_mass(m_loaded, unit=kilogram, precision=0)
    v_drive_str = fmt_velocity(v_drive, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    e_k_str = fmt_energy(e_k, unit=joule, precision=0)
```

The warehouse mobile manipulator that this book follows draws on all five. Loaded to at most `{python} MachineMomentum.m_loaded_str` and moving at its `{python} MachineMomentum.v_drive_str` drive limit (illustrative; see the Reader Guide), it carries `{python} MachineMomentum.e_k_str` of kinetic energy through aisles it shares with people.

Each budget becomes a limit established on the assembled machine under declared thermal and electrical stress. The first is the age of the measurement on which every command rests, which runs from physical transduction, before any software process receives the data.

## Measurement Freshness {#sec-body-measurement-freshness}

Software benchmarks in machine learning frequently report latency as isolated accelerator execution time (e.g., $18.5\text{ ms}$ for a vision backbone on an edge NPU), creating the dangerous illusion of a responsive $50\text{ Hz}$ control loop. In physical AI systems, however, that compute kernel is only one intermediate stage in an end-to-end silicon-to-plant dataflow pipeline. **A measurement decays continuously from the instant of physical transduction; what governs physical behavior is its total age when torque actually appears at the joint.** That physical age spans the interval from the moment photons strike a photodiode array, magnetic flux passes a Hall sensor, or strain deflects a piezoresistor to the moment motor inverter switches build stator magnetic flux that changes link acceleration. If a perception policy evaluates an obstacle bounding box in $18.5\text{ ms}$, but exposure integration, sensor readout, PCIe transport, kernel scheduling, fieldbus dispatch, and motor electrical current rise add another $40\text{ ms}$, the true physical age of the observation when the joint accelerates is nearly $60\text{ ms}$.

During that entire window, the continuous physical environment continues to evolve unobserved. In distributed data systems, read-after-write consistency windows govern whether a client acts on stale or linearized state. In Physical AI, the physical plant is an autonomous, unpausable concurrent writer: world state $\mathbf{x}(t)$ evolves along continuous trajectories at velocity $\mathbf{v}(t)$. An observation age $t_{\text{age}}$ converts directly into unobserved physical displacement $\Delta x \approx \int_0^{t_{\text{age}}} v(t)\,dt$. High-speed machines inevitably act on historical state.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ @Sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion derives how long a stored belief stays valid as its measurement ages.
:::

The rate of world-state change dictates how long a measurement remains valid before acting on it introduces intolerable error. Let $e_{\max}$ denote the maximum acceptable error in a tracked state, such as a joint angle or the position of a part on a conveyor, and let $v_{\max}$ denote the fastest credible velocity at which that state can evolve. The freshness deadline $\Delta t_{\text{fresh}}$ is the upper bound on measurement age before a control action based on that measurement becomes invalid, defined by the inequality
$$\Delta t_{\text{fresh}} \le \frac{e_{\max}}{v_{\max}}$$

For a vision-guided picker on a parcel sorter, tracking parcels at a maximum relative velocity $v_{\max} = 1.2\text{ m/s}$ with a geometric clearance tolerance $e_{\max} = 24\text{ mm}$, the freshness deadline is $24\text{ mm} / (1200\text{ mm/s}) = 20\text{ ms}$. If an actuation command reaches the motor based on an image captured $35\text{ ms}$ earlier, the parcel has displaced by $42\text{ mm}$, exceeding the position allowance by $18\text{ mm}$ and missing the grasp. The deadline governs a target that keeps moving while its measurement ages, such as the parcel here or the mug riding the mobile manipulator's pick-station conveyor. For such a target it limits only motion-induced error, and only while relative velocity is bounded and the initial observation is credible; sensing and estimation errors consume additional tolerance. Conversely, a stationary person standing in an aisle does not move while the observation ages; instead, the robot base moves toward the person, so the observation age converts into unguided vehicular travel before braking begins, which @sec-body-kinetic-momentum charges against the kinetic stopping budget.

### Transduction physics, quantization noise, and Nyquist limits {#sec-body-sensor-transduction}

Sensor selection spends both error tolerance and time. A sensor must resolve the motion of interest, and the filtering or scanning needed to obtain that resolution must fit the freshness deadline. Four mechanisms make this trade-off concrete:

1. **Optical Encoders and Velocity Quantization Noise:**
   An encoder measures joint angle in discrete increments. An $n$-bit encoder discretizes the continuous $2\pi$ radian circle into angular resolution $\delta \theta = \frac{2\pi}{2^n}$. For an 18-bit absolute encoder, $\delta \theta \approx 2.4 \times 10^{-5}\text{ rad}$ ($0.0014^\circ$); for a 12-bit magnetic encoder, $\delta \theta \approx 1.53 \times 10^{-3}\text{ rad}$ ($0.088^\circ$). Joint velocity must typically be estimated from successive angle samples across control cycle $\Delta t$:
   $$\dot{\theta}_k \approx \frac{\theta_k - \theta_{k-1}}{\Delta t}$$
   Backward differencing emphasizes rapid changes between samples, much as a high-pass filter does, so small angle errors can become large velocity errors when divided by a short sampling period. If successive quantization errors are independent and uniformly distributed over one encoder step, each has variance $(\delta\theta)^2/12$. Subtracting two such errors adds their variances, giving velocity-error standard deviation $\sigma_{\dot{\theta}} = \frac{\delta\theta}{\sqrt{6}\,\Delta t}$. This statistical model differs from a single count transition. At a $1\text{ kHz}$ servo loop ($\Delta t = 1\text{ ms}$), a one-count change of $1.53\text{ mrad}$ produces a velocity-estimate jump of $1.53\text{ rad/s}$ ($88^\circ/\text{s}$). If fed directly to velocity feedback or velocity-conditioned policy inputs, these jumps can provoke torque chatter and excite structural vibration. A low-pass filter smooths rapid sample changes, but that smoothing also delays the estimate's response to real motion. Filter selection must therefore balance noise suppression against the freshness budget.

2. **Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs) and Nyquist Aliasing:**
   An inertial measurement unit (IMU) measures acceleration and angular velocity. Sampling must distinguish the motion of interest from faster structural vibration. Under the Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem, a band-limited signal requires sampling above twice its highest frequency ($f_s > 2 f_{\max}$). Without adequate analog anti-aliasing filtering, vibrations above that range can appear as slower motion, misleading the state estimator. Raising the software update rate cannot recover information already aliased at the sensor.

3. **Tactile Sensor Arrays and Scanning Bandwidth:**
   Tactile arrays measure contact stress across a gripper through individual sensing elements called taxels. Scanning the elements one after another reduces wiring, but one frame then spans the whole scan, so the scan period adds directly to observation age and sets the fastest contact event, such as the onset of slip, that the array can resolve. More taxels at the same readout rate mean an older frame.

4. **Cameras and Rolling-Shutter Readout:**
   A rolling-shutter camera exposes and reads its pixel rows in sequence, so the rows of one frame differ in age by the full readout time, and motion during the readout shears the image. A frame's timestamp must therefore state which row, or which exposure midpoint, it represents. @Sec-perception-transduction-calibration sizes this skew on the mobile manipulator's navigation camera and removes it before the image reaches the estimator.

### The end-to-end sense-to-actuation latency pipeline {#sec-body-latency-pipeline}

```{python}
#| label: body-latency-profile-calc
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE PARCEL SORTER'S SENSE-TO-ACTUATION PROFILE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-02-latency-waterfall, @tbl-02-latency-breakdown, and the
# │          freshness-deadline paragraph of @sec-body-measurement-freshness.
# │ Goal:    Hold the illustrative stage profile in one place so the figure,
# │          the table, and the caption cannot disagree.
# │ Show:    20 ms deadline (24 mm at 1.2 m/s); stage P50 sum 35.0 ms, P99 sum
# │          50.0 ms, max sum 80.7 ms; system P99 46.2 ms and P99.9 68.4 ms;
# │          4.2 cm and 8.2 cm of parcel travel.
# │ How:     Stage sums; travel = v_max * age. Every stage value is
# │          illustrative: a measured profile of the integrated machine
# │          replaces it.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_length, check

class ParcelLatencyProfile:
    """Illustrative stage and end-to-end ages for the parcel-sorter picker."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    e_max = 24.0 * millimeter  # category: illustrative (grasp tolerance)
    v_max = 1.2 * meter / second  # category: illustrative (parcel speed)
    # (name, P50, P99, max) in ms; category: illustrative (not a measured profile)
    stages = [
        ("1–2. Exposure and readout", 11.2, 16.6, 16.7),
        ("3–4. Transport and DMA", 1.4, 3.2, 6.8),
        ("5. Backbone and policy", 18.5, 24.1, 38.4),
        ("6. Scheduling and IPC", 0.6, 2.1, 12.3),
        ("7. Fieldbus", 1.0, 1.0, 2.0),
        ("8. Current rise", 2.3, 3.0, 4.5),
    ]
    sys_p99 = 46.2 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (system-level profile)
    sys_p999 = 68.4 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (system-level tail)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_fresh = (e_max / v_max).to(millisecond)
    sum_p50 = sum(s[1] for s in stages) * millisecond
    sum_p99 = sum(s[2] for s in stages) * millisecond
    sum_max = sum(s[3] for s in stages) * millisecond
    travel_p50 = (v_max * sum_p50).to(millimeter)
    travel_p999 = (v_max * sys_p999).to(millimeter)
    excess_p50 = (travel_p50 - e_max).to(millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(t_fresh.magnitude - 20.0) < 1e-9, f"Freshness deadline drifted: {t_fresh}")
    check(abs(sum_p50.magnitude - 35.0) < 1e-9, f"P50 stage sum drifted: {sum_p50}")
    check(abs(sum_p99.magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, f"P99 stage sum drifted: {sum_p99}")
    check(abs(sum_max.magnitude - 80.7) < 1e-9, f"Max stage sum drifted: {sum_max}")
    check(sys_p99 < sum_p99, "The system P99 must differ from (here, sit below) the stage-P99 sum.")
    check(
        abs(travel_p50.magnitude - 42.0) < 1e-9 and abs(excess_p50.magnitude - 18.0) < 1e-9,
        "The freshness paragraph states 42 mm of travel, 18 mm past the tolerance.",
    )
    check(abs(travel_p999.magnitude - 82.08) < 1e-9, f"Tail travel drifted: {travel_p999}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    t_fresh_str = fmt_latency(t_fresh, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    sum_p50_str = fmt_latency(sum_p50, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    sum_p99_str = fmt_latency(sum_p99, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    sys_p99_str = fmt_latency(sys_p99, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    sys_p999_str = fmt_latency(sys_p999, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_backbone_str = fmt_latency(stages[2][1] * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    travel_p50_cm_str = fmt_length(travel_p50, unit=ureg.centimeter, precision=1)
    travel_p999_cm_str = fmt_length(travel_p999, unit=ureg.centimeter, precision=1)
```

::: {#fig-02-latency-waterfall fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Where a measurement's age comes from**: (a) The illustrative stages of @tbl-02-latency-breakdown laid end to end at their medians, with each stage's $P_{99}$ as a thin extension. The backbone's `{python} ParcelLatencyProfile.t_backbone_str` alone fits the parcel sorter's `{python} ParcelLatencyProfile.t_fresh_str` deadline; the stages around it do not. (b) The end-to-end age at the median, `{python} ParcelLatencyProfile.sum_p50_str`, and at $P_{99.9}$, `{python} ParcelLatencyProfile.sys_p999_str`, against that deadline; the shaded part of each bar is the overrun. At the parcel's speed they correspond to `{python} ParcelLatencyProfile.travel_p50_cm_str` and `{python} ParcelLatencyProfile.travel_p999_cm_str` of unguided motion." fig-alt="Two panels sharing a time axis in milliseconds from 0 to 85. Panel a: six horizontal bars, one per stage, placed end to end: exposure and readout, transport and DMA, backbone and policy, scheduling and IPC, fieldbus, and current rise, each with a thin extension to its 99th percentile. A red vertical line marks the 20 millisecond deadline; the median chain ends at 35 milliseconds. Panel b: two bars labeled median 35.0 milliseconds and 99.9th percentile 68.4 milliseconds, each shaded red beyond the 20 millisecond line, annotated 4.2 centimeters and 8.2 centimeters of travel."}

```{python}
#| label: fig-02-latency-waterfall
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SENSE-TO-ACTUATION WATERFALL (FIGURE)
# │ Context: @fig-02-latency-waterfall
# │ Goal:    show that the compute stage is a minority of the measurement's age
# │ Show:    six stages end to end at P50 with P99 extensions; P50 and P99.9
# │          end-to-end ages against the 20 ms deadline, overrun shaded
# │ How:     values from ParcelLatencyProfile (body-latency-profile-calc)
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import viz
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

P = ParcelLatencyProfile
R = viz.VOL4_ROLES
viz.set_book_style()
fig, (ax, bx) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(10, 5.0), sharex=True, gridspec_kw=dict(height_ratios=[3.2, 1.5], hspace=0.28))
roles = ["measured", "measured", "proposal", "structural", "structural", "neutral"]
dl = P.t_fresh.magnitude
t0 = 0.0
n = len(P.stages)
for k, ((name, p50, p99, _), role) in enumerate(zip(P.stages, roles)):
    y = n - 1 - k
    c = R[role]
    ax.barh(y, p50, left=t0, height=0.56, color=c, alpha=0.28, edgecolor=c, lw=1.0, zorder=3)
    ax.plot([t0 + p50, t0 + p99], [y, y], color=c, lw=1.4, zorder=3)
    ax.plot([t0 + p99, t0 + p99], [y - 0.14, y + 0.14], color=c, lw=1.4, zorder=3)
    ax.text(-1.0, y, name, ha="right", va="center", fontsize=9, color=R["neutral"])
    lab_x = t0 + max(p99, p50) + 1.0
    if lab_x > P.sum_p50.magnitude - 6:  # keep labels clear of the median-chain line
        lab_x = max(lab_x, P.sum_p50.magnitude + 0.8)
    ax.text(lab_x, y, f"{p50:.1f}", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=8.5, color=c)
    t0 += p50
ax.axvline(dl, color=R["consequence"], lw=1.2, zorder=2)
ax.text(dl + 0.6, n - 0.45, f"deadline {dl:.0f} ms", color=R["consequence"], fontsize=8.5, va="bottom")
ax.axvline(t0, color=R["neutral"], lw=0.9, ls="--", zorder=2)
ax.text(t0 + 0.6, n - 0.45, f"median chain {t0:g} ms", color=R["neutral"], fontsize=8.5, va="bottom")
ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_ylim(-0.6, n + 0.1)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
for side in ("left", "right", "top"):
    ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
ax.text(-0.26, 1.0, "(a)", transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=10.5, fontweight="bold", va="top")

rows = [
    (f"median {P.sum_p50.magnitude:g} ms", P.sum_p50.magnitude, P.travel_p50_cm_str),
    (f"$P_{{99.9}}$ {P.sys_p999.magnitude:.1f} ms", P.sys_p999.magnitude, P.travel_p999_cm_str),
]
for k, (name, age, travel) in enumerate(rows):
    y = 1 - k
    bx.barh(y, dl, left=0, height=0.55, color=R["neutral"], alpha=0.18, edgecolor=R["neutral"], lw=1.0, zorder=3)
    bx.barh(y, age - dl, left=dl, height=0.55, color=R["consequence"], alpha=0.22, edgecolor=R["consequence"], hatch="///", lw=1.0, zorder=3)
    bx.text(-1.0, y, name, ha="right", va="center", fontsize=9, color=R["neutral"])
    bx.text(age + 1.0, y, f"{travel} of travel", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=8.5, color=R["consequence"])
bx.axvline(dl, color=R["consequence"], lw=1.2, zorder=4)
bx.set_yticks([])
bx.set_ylim(-0.6, 1.6)
bx.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
for side in ("left", "right", "top"):
    bx.spines[side].set_visible(False)
bx.set_xlim(0, 85)
bx.set_xlabel("Age of the measurement (ms)")
bx.text(-0.26, 1.0, "(b)", transform=bx.transAxes, fontsize=10.5, fontweight="bold", va="top")
plt.show()
```
:::

@Fig-02-latency-waterfall lays the path from photon to torque end to end. Before inference, the sensor integrates its exposure and reads out its rows over MIPI CSI-2, direct memory access (DMA) moves the frame into host memory, and the kernel hands it to user space. After inference, inter-process communication (IPC) carries the proposal to the safety microcontroller, the EtherCAT fieldbus delivers it to the drive, and gate-drive switching builds the stator flux that produces torque. Judged against the `{python} ParcelLatencyProfile.t_fresh_str` freshness deadline, neural inference alone takes only `{python} ParcelLatencyProfile.t_backbone_str` at the median, yet the stages before and after it push the median end-to-end age to `{python} ParcelLatencyProfile.sum_p50_str`, `{python} ParcelLatencyProfile.travel_p50_cm_str` of unguided parcel motion. Under queue congestion and memory bus contention, the $P_{99.9}$ tail reaches `{python} ParcelLatencyProfile.sys_p999_str`, `{python} ParcelLatencyProfile.travel_p999_cm_str` of motion, more than three times the tolerance budget. A benchmark that times only the backbone measures the one stage that fits.

Engineers often compute total latency by summing the $P_{99}$ values of individual stages, but the percentile of a sum is not the sum of the percentiles.[^fn-math-quantile-convolution] In embedded system-on-chip (SoC) architectures, shared system bus contention (such as PCIe DMA bursts saturating memory controllers during camera readout), memory bandwidth throttling on edge accelerators, and kernel thread preemption correlate stage delays. The distribution of complete sense-to-torque age must therefore be profiled empirically on the integrated machine under declared multi-tenant compute loads, and even that measured percentile is not the analyzed bound a hard safety deadline demands (@sec-nervous-deterministic-fieldbuses).

[^fn-math-quantile-convolution]: **Quantile Convolution**\index{Quantile convolution!tail non-additivity}: In general, the quantile of a latency sum differs from the sum of equal-percentile stage quantiles ($Q_p(X + Y) \ne Q_p(X) + Q_p(Y)$). Independence alone does not make their arithmetic sum a worst-case bound. Correlation from shared buses and queues changes the end-to-end tail and must be characterized at the system boundary.

The stage timings behind the figure (@tbl-02-latency-breakdown), profiled on the camera-to-joint path under continuous inference load, show the gap between the two ways of adding.

| Pipeline Stage                     | Physical Mechanism / Contention Source                           | $P_{50}$ (ms) | $P_{99}$ (ms) | Max (ms) |
|:-----------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------:|:-------------:|:--------:|
| **1–2. Sensor Exposure & Readout** | $60\text{ Hz}$ rolling shutter exposure midpoint                 |     $11.2$    |     $16.6$    |  $16.7$  |
| **3–4. Host Transport & DMA**      | PCIe DMA transfer into host memory                               |     $1.4$     |     $3.2$     |  $6.8$   |
| **5. Vision Backbone & Policy**    | Onboard accelerator inference (memory throttling tail)           |     $18.5$    |     $24.1$    |  $38.4$  |
| **6. OS Scheduling & IPC**         | Kernel preemption and mailbox dispatch to safety microcontroller |     $0.6$     |     $2.1$     |  $12.3$  |
| **7. Fieldbus Transmission**       | Deterministic EtherCAT cyclic packet exchange                    |     $1.0$     |     $1.0$     |  $2.0$   |
| **8. Actuator Current Rise**       | Gate driver switching and stator flux buildup                    |     $2.3$     |     $3.0$     |  $4.5$   |
| **Arithmetic Stage Sum**           | Sum of each column's stage values; not an end-to-end quantile    |    **35.0**   |    **50.0**   | **80.7** |
| **End-to-End Age**                 | System-level profile ($t_{\text{transduction}} \to \tau$)        |    **35.0**   |    **46.2**   | **80.7** |

: **Illustrative sense-to-actuation latency decomposition**: Stage and system-level timings show why the arithmetic sum of stage percentiles is not the end-to-end tail. The example's $P_{99.9} = 68.4\text{ ms}$ exceeds the $20\text{ ms}$ freshness deadline of the parcel sorter. {#tbl-02-latency-breakdown tbl-colwidths="[26,38,12,12,12]"}

The `{python} ParcelLatencyProfile.sum_p99_str` sum of stage $P_{99}$ values differs from the `{python} ParcelLatencyProfile.sys_p99_str` system percentile, and against the `{python} ParcelLatencyProfile.t_fresh_str` deadline even the `{python} ParcelLatencyProfile.sum_p50_str` median would be late.

Late feedback can also reinforce a tracking error instead of correcting it,[^fn-math-bode-delay] but the freshness calculation needs no frequency-domain model: the parcel has already moved beyond the allowed tolerance. The architecture must preserve the observation's physical capture time. Hardware timestamps synchronized through **IEEE 802.1AS**\index{IEEE 802.1AS!hardware timestamping}, the generalized Precision Time Protocol (gPTP),[^fn-hw-gptp-timestamp] or capture strobes associated with the **MIPI CSI-2**\index{MIPI CSI-2!sensor readout interface}[^fn-hw-mipi-capture] interface provide a timing reference; the sensor's exposure and readout behavior determine how that reference maps to the measurement. The timestamp then travels with the observation through computation.

Before committing a proposal to actuator registers, the permission path compares observation age $t_{\text{age}} = t_{\text{now}} - t_{\text{transduction}}$ with the freshness deadline, reserving time for the remaining actuator response. If $t_{\text{age}} > \Delta t_{\text{fresh}}$, it refuses that proposal. An already active command may continue only while its own evidence and permission remain valid; otherwise the path invokes a qualified fallback within the remaining physical margin [@brooks1986robust]. Refusing a stale replacement and ending valid ongoing motion are separate decisions.

[^fn-math-bode-delay]: **Transport Delay and Feedback Stability**\index{Transport delay!feedback instability}\index{Asynchronous divergence!closed-loop}: Transport delay makes a controller act on historical state. Whether delayed corrections destabilize the loop depends on the plant, controller, and total response. @Sec-appendix-control-zoh develops the phase-margin calculation; delay alone does not establish a particular oscillation or damage outcome.

[^fn-hw-gptp-timestamp]: **IEEE 802.1AS (gPTP)**\index{IEEE 802.1AS!hardware timestamping}\index{IEEE 1588!Precision Time Protocol}: The generalized Precision Time Protocol of IEEE 802.1AS is a profile of the IEEE 1588 Precision Time Protocol for time-sensitive Ethernet networks [@ieee8021as2020]. It synchronizes clocks by exchanging packets timestamped in hardware at the network interface, which keeps the operating-system scheduler's jitter out of the measurement.

[^fn-hw-mipi-capture]: **MIPI CSI-2**\index{MIPI CSI-2!sensor readout interface}: The Mobile Industry Processor Interface Camera Serial Interface 2 (MIPI CSI-2) is a high-bandwidth, high-speed differential protocol used for transmitting uncompressed video data directly from image sensors to host system-on-chip (SoC) devices with minimal latency.

::: {.callout-perspective title="The publish timestamp anti-pattern"}
A common architectural defect in robotics software is timestamping sensor observations inside user-space publishers (such as a ROS 2 or DDS node). Doing so discards exposure midpoint, rolling-shutter integration, sensor readout, DMA transfers, and kernel queue latency, which removes the first four stages of @tbl-02-latency-breakdown from the age calculation. Timestamps must be latched at the physical transducer via hardware strobes at the silicon interface (such as MIPI CSI-2 Start-of-Frame or Ethernet PHY hardware timestamps synchronized through IEEE 802.1AS) before data enters operating-system queues.
:::

Throughout that sense-to-actuation interval, the body continues moving, carrying momentum that no software interrupt can cancel.

## Kinetic Momentum {#sec-body-kinetic-momentum}

```{python}
#| label: body-stopping-budget-calc
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE BODY'S STOPPING DISTANCE ON THE RUNNING MACHINE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-body-kinetic-momentum opener, @fig-02-stopping-distance, and
# │          \ref{nbk-body-stopping-distance-budgeting-high-tail-compute}.
# │ Goal:    Add the body's own terms of @eq-body-stopping-distance for the
# │          loaded warehouse mobile manipulator at its drive limit.
# │ Show:    Rows 1-3 of the stopping budget at 1.5 m/s: braking 562.5 mm,
# │          overhead 150 mm (712.5), brake onset 30 mm (742.5), leaving 357.5 mm
# │          of the 1.10 m clear distance; body-only ceiling 1.91 m/s; at 2.0 m/s
# │          braking is 1000 mm (+77.8 percent); each extra 100 ms adds 150 mm;
# │          figure cases 742.5 / 912.9 / 1417.2 mm.
# │ How:     calc_safe_stopping_distance and calc_max_permitted_velocity with
# │          a_eff = a_brake (constant deceleration), from RM and AISLE. The full
# │          pre-brake delay AISLE.tau_delay appears only in the figure's cases.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import (
    fmt_mass,
    fmt_length,
    fmt_energy,
    fmt_latency,
    fmt_velocity,
    fmt_acceleration,
    fmt_percent,
    fmt_display_math,
    check,
)

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class BodyStoppingBudget:
    """Rows 1-3 of the running machine's stopping budget: the terms the body owns."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative (drive limit)
    a_brake = AISLE.a_brake  # category: illustrative (loaded, dry floor)
    delta_loc = AISLE.delta_loc  # category: illustrative
    delta_margin = AISLE.delta_margin  # category: chosen
    t_act = AISLE.t_brake_onset  # category: illustrative (brake onset)
    d_clear = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative (rack-end clear distance)
    tau_full = AISLE.tau_delay  # category: derived (full pre-brake delay; figure only)
    v_fast = 2.0 * meter / second  # category: illustrative (speed-scaling case above the drive limit)
    dt_extra = 100 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (added pre-brake delay step)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    d_brake = (v**2 / (2 * a_brake)).to(ureg.millimeter)  # row 1
    total_1 = d_brake
    overhead = (delta_loc + delta_margin).to(ureg.millimeter)  # row 2
    total_2 = (total_1 + overhead).to(ureg.millimeter)
    d_onset = (v * t_act).to(ureg.millimeter)  # row 3
    total_3 = (total_2 + d_onset).to(ureg.millimeter)
    remaining = (d_clear - total_3).to(ureg.millimeter)
    v_ceiling = calc_max_permitted_velocity(d_clear, t_act, a_brake, loc_margin=delta_loc, physical_margin=delta_margin)
    d_brake_fast = (v_fast**2 / (2 * a_brake)).to(ureg.millimeter)
    brake_growth = (d_brake_fast / d_brake - 1).to("dimensionless")
    d_per_extra = (v * dt_extra).to(ureg.millimeter)
    case_body = calc_safe_stopping_distance(v, t_act, a_brake, loc_margin=delta_loc, physical_margin=delta_margin).to(ureg.millimeter)
    case_full = calc_safe_stopping_distance(v, tau_full, a_brake, loc_margin=delta_loc, physical_margin=delta_margin).to(ureg.millimeter)
    case_fast = calc_safe_stopping_distance(v_fast, tau_full, a_brake, loc_margin=delta_loc, physical_margin=delta_margin).to(ureg.millimeter)
    case_full_blind = (v * tau_full).to(ureg.millimeter)
    case_full_margin = (d_clear - case_full).to(ureg.millimeter)
    case_fast_blind = (v_fast * tau_full).to(ureg.millimeter)
    case_fast_breach = (case_fast - d_clear).to(ureg.millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(v == MachineMomentum.v_drive, "Stopping budget and momentum must use the same drive limit.")
    check(abs(total_1.magnitude - 562.5) < 1e-6, f"Row 1 must be 562.5 mm: {total_1}")
    check(abs(total_2.magnitude - 712.5) < 1e-6, f"Row 2 running total must be 712.5 mm: {total_2}")
    check(abs(total_3.magnitude - 742.5) < 1e-6, f"Ch2 subtotal must be 742.5 mm: {total_3}")
    check(abs(case_body.magnitude - total_3.magnitude) < 1e-6, "Row sum must equal the equation.")
    check(abs(remaining.magnitude - 357.5) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected remaining clearance: {remaining}")
    check(abs(v_ceiling.magnitude - 1.9098) < 1e-4, f"Body-only ceiling must be 1.9098 m/s: {v_ceiling}")
    check(v_ceiling > v, "The body-only ceiling must exceed the drive limit.")
    check(abs(d_brake_fast.magnitude - 1000.0) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected braking at 2.0 m/s: {d_brake_fast}")
    check(abs(d_per_extra.magnitude - 150.0) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected cost of 100 ms: {d_per_extra}")
    check(abs(tau_full.to(millisecond).magnitude - 133.6) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected tau_delay: {tau_full}")
    check(abs(case_full.magnitude - 912.9) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected full-delay case: {case_full}")
    check(abs(case_fast.magnitude - 1417.2) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected fast case: {case_fast}")
    check(case_full < d_clear < case_fast, "Case 2 must fit and Case 3 must breach the clear distance.")
    check(abs(case_full_blind.magnitude - 200.4) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected case_full_blind: {case_full_blind}")
    check(abs(case_full_margin.magnitude - 187.1) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected case_full_margin: {case_full_margin}")
    check(abs(case_fast_blind.magnitude - 267.2) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected case_fast_blind: {case_fast_blind}")
    check(abs(case_fast_breach.magnitude - 317.2) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected case_fast_breach: {case_fast_breach}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    a_brake_str = fmt_acceleration(a_brake, unit=meter / second**2, precision=0)
    delta_loc_str = fmt_length(delta_loc, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    delta_margin_str = fmt_length(delta_margin, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    t_act_str = fmt_latency(t_act, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(d_clear, unit=meter, precision=2)
    tau_full_str = fmt_latency(tau_full, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    v_fast_str = fmt_velocity(v_fast, unit=meter / second, precision=0)
    dt_extra_str = fmt_latency(dt_extra, unit=millisecond, precision=0)

    d_brake_str = fmt_length(d_brake, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    overhead_str = fmt_length(overhead, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    total_2_str = fmt_length(total_2, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    d_onset_str = fmt_length(d_onset, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    total_3_str = fmt_length(total_3, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    remaining_str = fmt_length(remaining, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    v_ceiling_str = fmt_velocity(v_ceiling, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    d_brake_fast_str = fmt_length(d_brake_fast, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0, commas=True)
    brake_growth_pct_str = fmt_percent(brake_growth.magnitude, precision=1, style="prose")
    d_per_extra_str = fmt_length(d_per_extra, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    case_body_str = fmt_length(case_body, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    case_full_str = fmt_length(case_full, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    case_fast_str = fmt_length(case_fast, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1, commas=True)
    _case_full_blind_str = fmt_length(case_full_blind, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    _case_full_margin_str = fmt_length(case_full_margin, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    _case_fast_blind_str = fmt_length(case_fast_blind, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    _case_fast_breach_str = fmt_length(case_fast_breach, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)

    d_brake_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"d_{{\text{{brake}}}} = \frac{{v^2}}{{2 a_{{\text{{brake}}}}}} = \frac{{({v_str})^2}}{{2 \times {a_brake_str}}} = {d_brake_str}"
    )
    overhead_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"\delta_{{\text{{loc}}}} + \delta_{{\text{{margin}}}} = {delta_loc_str} + {delta_margin_str} = {overhead_str}"
    )
    d_onset_display_math = fmt_display_math(rf"v\,T_{{\text{{act}}}} = ({v_str}) \times ({t_act_str}) = {d_onset_str}")
    total_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"d_{{\text{{stop}}}}\big|_{{\text{{body}}}} = {d_brake_str} + {overhead_str} + {d_onset_str} = {total_3_str}"
    )
    ceiling_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"v_{{\max}} = -a_{{\text{{brake}}}} T_{{\text{{act}}}} + \sqrt{{(a_{{\text{{brake}}}} T_{{\text{{act}}}})^2 + 2 a_{{\text{{brake}}}} (D_{{\text{{clear}}}} - \delta_{{\text{{loc}}}} - \delta_{{\text{{margin}}}})}} \approx {v_ceiling_str}"
    )
```

The loaded mobile manipulator drives down an aisle at its `{python} BodyStoppingBudget.v_str` drive limit. A person steps out from the end of a rack `{python} BodyStoppingBudget.d_clear_str` ahead and stands in the aisle. Software cannot simply abort execution or instantaneously zero the velocity vector: in physical AI, moving mass carries kinetic momentum ($p = mv$) and kinetic energy ($E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$) that cannot be reclaimed by a garbage collector or flushed from memory registers. Bringing that mass to rest requires dissipating kinetic energy across physical distance through mechanical work ($W = \int F \, dx$). **Stopping distance grows linearly with delay and quadratically with speed, and that scaling asymmetry sets the machine's physical execution roofline.**

### Kinematic stopping distance and pre-brake delay {#sec-body-stopping-distance-prebrake}

From the observation that first captures a stationary hazard to rest, the modeled stop comprises two phases: pre-brake travel and braking travel. The pre-brake delay $\tau_{\text{delay}}$ covers the applicable sensing, decision, communication, and actuator-onset intervals. A proposal-dependent response includes its computation; an independent protective response need not wait for that computation. The budget must follow the path that actually initiates braking. If the hazard can appear between observations, the time until capture also needs an allowance. During the modeled delay, we conservatively credit no retarding force and assume approximately constant speed $v$, giving
$$d_{\text{blind}} = v\,\tau_{\text{delay}}$$

Once the selected braking mechanism develops retarding force, the body enters the braking phase. The mechanical work done by retarding braking force $F_{\text{brake}}$ across physical braking distance\index{Braking distance} $d_{\text{brake}}$ removes the machine's stored kinetic energy, $W = \Delta E_k$. A powered motor stop requires functioning drive electronics and a path to absorb or dissipate returned energy; a mechanical brake has its own onset and stopping characteristics. The credible deceleration belongs to the mechanism actually available in the fault being analyzed.

```{python}
#| label: body-braking-limits-calc
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CAN THE DRIVES DELIVER THE CREDIBLE DECELERATION? (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: the rotating-mass paragraph and the three ceilings in
# │          @sec-body-stopping-distance-prebrake, \ref{nbk-body-braking-drive-limits}
# │          in @sec-body-electrical-time-constants, and the drive-torque column
# │          of @tbl-02-limit-record.
# │ Goal:    Check a_brake = 2.0 m/s^2 against traction, tip-over, and the
# │          torque of the sourced hub-motor drives, and check back-EMF
# │          headroom at the drive limit.
# │ Show:    traction needs mu >= 0.204 with all weight on the driven wheels,
# │          >= 0.250 at the 300 kg/pair load rating; inspected floor gives
# │          1.18 m/s^2; tip-over needs h_cg/d <= 4.90 (CoG needs source);
# │          60 N m per wheel -> 902 N, m_eff <= 387 kg -> >= 2.33 m/s^2
# │          (16.6 percent above), 0.78 m/s^2 at rated current; 108 rpm,
# │          e = 28.2 V, braking needs 10.7 V, driving 45.7 V > 42 V.
# │ How:     calc_braking_limits, calc_drive_torque_deceleration_limit,
# │          calc_required_friction, calc_drive_voltage_headroom with
# │          RM.drive_unit (ZLTECH ZLLG10ASM800 datasheet) and RM.drive_bus_*.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import (
    fmt,
    fmt_int,
    fmt_mass,
    fmt_length,
    fmt_force,
    fmt_torque,
    fmt_torque_constant,
    fmt_acceleration,
    fmt_velocity,
    fmt_voltage,
    fmt_current,
    fmt_resistance,
    fmt_percent,
    fmt_angular_velocity,
    check,
)

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class BrakingLimits:
    """Traction, tip-over, drive-torque, and back-EMF checks on the credible deceleration."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    m = RM.loaded_mass  # category: derived (upper bound, full tote rack)
    a_req = AISLE.a_brake  # category: illustrative (credible loaded deceleration)
    v = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative (drive limit)
    hub = RM.drive_unit  # category: sourced (ZLTECH ZLLG10ASM800 datasheet)
    n_wheels = RM.drive_wheel_count  # category: chosen (two driven wheels, casters elsewhere)
    r_wheel = hub.wheel_radius  # category: sourced (266 mm wheel)
    k_t = hub.torque_constant  # category: derived (datasheet peak torque / peak current)
    i_max = RM.drive_current_limit  # category: chosen (the motor's datasheet peak current)
    tau_rated = hub.rated_torque  # category: sourced (at the rated current)
    i_rated = hub.rated_current  # category: sourced
    m_rot_wheel = hub.rotating_mass_bound  # category: sourced (motor mass bounds J / r^2; rotor inertia needs source)
    k_e = hub.back_emf_constant  # category: sourced (line-to-line)
    r_line = hub.line_resistance  # category: sourced (line-to-line)
    load_pair = hub.load_rating_per_pair  # category: sourced
    v_bus_low = RM.drive_bus_battery_low  # category: sourced (48 V-class pack minimum)
    mu_dry = AISLE.mu_dry  # category: illustrative
    mu_insp = AISLE.mu_inspected_floor  # category: illustrative

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    tau_wheel = (k_t * i_max).to(ureg.newton * meter)
    m_rot = (n_wheels * m_rot_wheel).to(kilogram)
    rot_share = (m_rot / m).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    phi_max = RM.drive_wheel_load_share_max
    limits = calc_braking_limits(
        m,
        a_req,
        wheel_torque_max=tau_wheel,
        wheel_radius=r_wheel,
        n_driven_wheels=n_wheels,
        friction_coefficient=mu_dry,
        drive_load_share=phi_max,
        rotating_equivalent_mass=m_rot,
    )
    force = limits["force"]
    m_eff = limits["m_eff"]
    a_torque = limits["a_torque"]
    torque_margin = (a_torque / a_req - 1).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    a_torque_rated = calc_drive_torque_deceleration_limit(tau_rated, r_wheel, n_wheels, m, m_rot)["a_max"]
    mu_min = calc_required_friction(a_req)
    mu_min_rated = limits["mu_required"]
    phi_min_dry = (a_req / (mu_dry * ureg.standard_gravity)).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    a_insp = calc_traction_deceleration_limit(mu_insp)
    cg_ratio_max = limits["cg_ratio_max"]
    volts = calc_drive_voltage_headroom(k_e, v, r_wheel, v_bus_low, i_max, r_line)
    omega = volts["omega"]
    e_bemf = volts["e_bemf"]
    v_brake = volts["v_brake"]
    v_drive = volts["v_drive"]
    headroom = volts["headroom"]

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(n_wheels == 2, f"Prose says two driven wheels: {n_wheels}")
    check(abs(tau_wheel.magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-9, f"Wheel torque at the limit must be 60 N m: {tau_wheel}")
    check(abs(force.magnitude - 902.26) < 0.01, f"Unexpected retarding force: {force}")
    check(abs(m_eff.magnitude - 387.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected effective-mass bound: {m_eff}")
    check(abs(a_torque.magnitude - 2.3314) < 1e-4, f"Unexpected torque ceiling: {a_torque}")
    check(a_torque > a_req, "The drive-torque ceiling must clear the credible deceleration.")
    check(a_torque_rated < a_req, "At rated current the drives must fall short of a_brake.")
    check(abs(mu_min - 0.204) < 5e-4, f"Friction premise must be 0.204: {mu_min}")
    check(abs(phi_max - 300.0 / 368.0) < 1e-12, f"Unexpected load-share bound: {phi_max}")
    check(abs(mu_min_rated - 0.2502) < 1e-4, f"Unexpected rated-share friction premise: {mu_min_rated}")
    check(mu_dry > mu_min_rated and a_insp < a_req, "Dry floor must pass and the inspected floor must fail.")
    check(limits["a_tip"] is None and limits["passes"] is False, "Tip-over must stay unverified until the CoG is sourced.")
    check(abs(cg_ratio_max - 4.9033) < 1e-4, f"Unexpected CoG ratio bound: {cg_ratio_max}")
    check(abs(e_bemf.magnitude - 28.217) < 1e-3, f"Unexpected back-EMF: {e_bemf}")
    check(0 * volt < v_brake < v_bus_low < v_drive, "Braking must fit the depleted bus; driving at peak current must not.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    m_str = fmt_mass(m, unit=kilogram, precision=0)
    a_req_str = fmt_acceleration(a_req, unit=meter / second**2, precision=0)
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    r_wheel_str = fmt_length(r_wheel, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    k_t_str = fmt_torque_constant(k_t, precision=1)
    i_max_str = fmt_current(i_max, unit=ureg.ampere, precision=0)
    i_rated_str = fmt_current(i_rated, unit=ureg.ampere, precision=1)
    tau_rated_str = fmt_torque(tau_rated, precision=0)
    tau_wheel_str = fmt_torque(tau_wheel, precision=0)
    force_str = fmt_force(force, precision=1)
    m_rot_wheel_str = fmt_mass(m_rot_wheel, unit=kilogram, precision=1)
    m_eff_str = fmt_mass(m_eff, unit=kilogram, precision=0)
    rot_pct_str = fmt_percent(rot_share, precision=1, style="prose")
    a_torque_str = fmt_acceleration(a_torque, unit=meter / second**2, precision=2)
    torque_margin_pct_str = fmt_percent(torque_margin, precision=1, style="prose")
    torque_margin_pct_sym_str = fmt_percent(torque_margin, precision=1, style="symbol")
    a_torque_rated_str = fmt_acceleration(a_torque_rated, unit=meter / second**2, precision=2)
    mu_min_str = fmt(mu_min, precision=3)
    load_pair_str = fmt_mass(load_pair, unit=kilogram, precision=0)
    phi_max_str = fmt(phi_max, precision=3)
    mu_min_rated_str = fmt(mu_min_rated, precision=3)
    mu_dry_str = fmt(mu_dry, precision=2)
    phi_min_dry_str = fmt(phi_min_dry, precision=2)
    mu_insp_str = fmt(mu_insp, precision=2)
    a_insp_str = fmt_acceleration(a_insp, unit=meter / second**2, precision=2)
    cg_ratio_max_str = fmt(cg_ratio_max, precision=2)
    omega_str = fmt_angular_velocity(omega, unit=ureg.rpm, precision=1)
    e_bemf_str = fmt_voltage(e_bemf, unit=volt, precision=1)
    r_line_str = fmt_resistance(r_line, unit=ureg.ohm, precision=1)
    v_brake_str = fmt_voltage(v_brake, unit=volt, precision=1)
    v_drive_str = fmt_voltage(v_drive, unit=volt, precision=1)
    v_bus_low_str = fmt_voltage(v_bus_low, unit=volt, precision=0)
    headroom_str = fmt_voltage(headroom, unit=volt, precision=1)
```

In an embodied machine, stored kinetic energy includes the spinning parts as well as the translating chassis. A part spinning at angular velocity $\omega$ stores $\frac{1}{2} J \omega^2$, where its moment of inertia $J$ (in $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$) plays the role that mass plays in $\frac{1}{2} m v^2$: it measures how strongly the part resists a change in its rotation speed. A transmission with **gear ratio**\index{Gear ratio!definition} $N$ turns the motor $N$ times for every turn of its output, multiplying the motor's torque by $N$ and dividing its speed by $N$. The machine's kinetic energy is therefore the translational energy of the chassis and payload ($E_{k,\text{trans}} = \frac{1}{2} m v^2$) plus the rotational energy of its wheels, gearboxes, and motor rotors ($E_{k,\text{rot}} = \sum_i \frac{1}{2} J_{\text{rotor}, i} \omega_{i}^2$). Because a drive of ratio $N_i$ spins its rotor at $\omega_i = N_i \frac{v}{r_{\text{wheel}}}$, the rotor's rotational kinetic energy reflects into the translational domain scaled by the square of the gear ratio:
$$E_{k,\text{total}} = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 + \sum_i \frac{1}{2} J_{\text{rotor}, i} \left(N_i \frac{v}{r_{\text{wheel}}}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{2} \left(m + \sum_i \frac{N_i^2 J_{\text{rotor}, i}}{r_{\text{wheel}}^2}\right) v^2$$
This formulation reveals that the effective translational inertia of the machine is $m_{\text{eff}} = m + \sum_i \frac{N_i^2 J_{\text{rotor}, i}}{r_{\text{wheel}}^2}$. For a machine decelerating to rest under sustained retarding force $F_{\text{brake}} = m_{\text{eff}} a_{\text{brake}}$, the work-energy theorem balances mechanical work against total kinetic energy:
$$m_{\text{eff}} a_{\text{brake}} d_{\text{brake}} = \frac{1}{2} m_{\text{eff}} v^2$$
Dividing by effective mass yields the kinematic braking travel:
$$d_{\text{brake}} = \frac{v^2}{2 a_{\text{brake}}}$$
If an engineer evaluates braking capacity using bare chassis mass alone ($a_{\text{nominal}} = F_{\text{brake}} / m$), they ignore the kinetic energy stored in the spinning motor rotors, overestimating deceleration by the factor $m_{\text{eff}} / m$ and underestimating stopping travel by $\frac{m_{\text{eff}} - m}{m} = \sum_i \frac{N_i^2 J_{\text{rotor}, i}}{m r_{\text{wheel}}^2}$. On the running machine the correction is small. Its two driven wheels are direct-drive hub motors ($N_i = 1$), and although their datasheet omits rotor inertia, no part of a hub motor lies outside its tire, so each $J_i/r_{\text{wheel}}^2$ cannot exceed the motor's `{python} BrakingLimits.m_rot_wheel_str` mass. The rotating parts add at most `{python} BrakingLimits.rot_pct_str` to the `{python} BrakingLimits.m_str` loaded mass. Because the correction grows with $N_i^2$, it matters most on light platforms driven through high-ratio gearboxes.

The parameter $a_{\text{brake}}$ is the credible sustained deceleration the physical plant can exert against the environment, not an idealized rating copied from an actuator datasheet. The retarding force $F_{\text{brake}} = m_{\text{eff}} a_{\text{brake}}$ must fit under three independent ceilings. Traction bounds it at the floor. Only the braked wheels push against the floor, and friction there can reach at most $\mu$ times the normal force they carry, $\phi_{\text{drive}} m g$, so $a_{\text{brake}} \le \mu g \phi_{\text{drive}}$, where $\mu$ is the tire-floor friction coefficient and $\phi_{\text{drive}}$ is the fraction of the weight those wheels carry. Tip-over bounds it through the mass distribution. The braking force acts at the floor while inertia acts at the center of gravity, a height $h_{\text{cg}}$ above it. Taking moments about the leading support, a horizontal distance $d$ ahead of the center of gravity, the inertial moment $m a_{\text{brake}} h_{\text{cg}}$ tries to pitch the body forward and the weight's moment $m g d$ holds it down, so the body stays on its wheels only while $a_{\text{brake}} \le g\,d/h_{\text{cg}}$. Raising or extending the arm changes both terms, so this ceiling depends on the machine's state. The drives bound it through the largest torque their current limit allows, a ceiling that @sec-body-electrical-time-constants derives from the motor's torque per ampere. If an engineer restricts inverter current limits, or if back-EMF, the voltage a spinning motor generates against its own supply, leaves the inverter too little headroom to control current, the drive cannot deliver the required braking torque, silently degrading $a_{\text{brake}}$ and expanding braking travel without software notification. The rotor's own inertia is already counted in $m_{\text{eff}}$ and must not be charged a second time. @Fig-02-braking-fbd draws the three ceilings on the loaded base, and \ref{nbk-body-braking-drive-limits} checks them on the running machine.

```{python}
#| label: body-braking-fbd-guard

#| warning: false

# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ BRAKING FREE-BODY DIAGRAM (LEGO GUARD FOR A HAND-DRAWN FIGURE)
```

The constant-deceleration model requires a level surface and a qualified braking response. A conservative approximation can charge the interval until sustained deceleration is available to $\tau_{\text{delay}}$, then use a lower bound $a_{\text{brake}}$. The brake-onset allowance ($T_{\text{act}}$) enters that delay once. A later calculation that models a finite torque ramp must reconcile its ramp travel with this allowance rather than add the same interval twice. Loaded stopping trials across declared conditions establish the applicable response, uncertainty, and margin; a sample percentile alone is not a certified lower bound.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Unmanaged kinetic momentum translates directly into the destructive contact shock loads analyzed in @sec-body-actuator-limits.
:::

The differing exponents of the blind-travel and braking terms make velocity the dominant multiplier of spatial risk (@fig-02-stopping-distance), a scaling that \ref{nbk-body-stopping-distance-budgeting-high-tail-compute} works numerically.

In unstructured environments, a machine cannot allocate its entire clearance to nominal stopping dynamics. Obstacle tracking carries state estimation uncertainty, sensor calibration drifts over time, and localization algorithms introduce position error. The stopping distance $d_{\text{stop}}$ that the system defends must therefore include a spatial localization uncertainty bound $\delta_{\text{loc}}$ and a minimum physical clearance margin $\delta_{\text{margin}}$:[^fn-std-iso-separation]

$$d_{\text{stop}} = v\,\tau_{\text{delay}} + \frac{v^2}{2 a_{\text{brake}}} + \delta_{\text{loc}} + \delta_{\text{margin}}$$ {#eq-body-stopping-distance}

The sum $\delta_{\text{loc}} + \delta_{\text{margin}}$ is fixed spatial overhead that must remain unoccupied when the body comes to a complete rest.

[^fn-std-iso-separation]: **Protective Separation Distance**\index{ISO/TS 15066!separation distance}\index{Speed and Separation Monitoring}\index{ISO 3691-4!mobile base}: ISO 10218-2:2025 incorporates the collaborative-application requirements formerly published as ISO/TS 15066; ISO/TS 15066:2016 itself remains published and is under revision, and for speed and separation monitoring (SSM) of robot arms it writes the protective separation distance as $S_p = S_h + S_r + S_s + C + Z_d + Z_r$: the person's travel $S_h$ over the robot's reaction and stopping times, the robot's travel during its reaction time $S_r$, its stopping distance $S_s$, an intrusion distance $C$ set by what the sensing can detect, and the position uncertainties of the person ($Z_d$) and the robot ($Z_r$) [@isots15066; @iso10218part2; @marvel2017implementing]. The robot's terms map onto @eq-body-stopping-distance, with $v\,\tau_{\text{delay}}$ as $S_r$, $v^2/2a_{\text{brake}}$ as $S_s$, and $\delta_{\text{loc}}$ as $Z_r$. ISO 10218-2:2025 does not address the hazards of mobility when a manipulator rides on a mobile platform, and a mobile base's protective fields fall under ISO 3691-4:2023 for driverless industrial trucks [@iso3691part4]. For a learned policy, an unbounded compute tail lengthens the reaction time, which enlarges both $S_h$ and $S_r$ and forces the protective field outward.

::: {#dfn-body-dynamic-stopping-distance .callout-definition title="Dynamic stopping distance"}

***Dynamic stopping distance***\index{Dynamic stopping distance!definition}\index{Stopping distance!definition} ($d_{\text{stop}}$) is the minimum physical clearance required to bring a moving mass to a complete halt from its speed $v$ when the hazard is first imaged. It sums the travel during the pre-brake delay $\tau_{\text{delay}}$, which runs from the exposure of the frame that shows the hazard until retarding force begins; the braking travel under the credible deceleration $a_{\text{brake}}$; and the localization bound $\delta_{\text{loc}}$ and protective clearance $\delta_{\text{margin}}$, as @eq-body-stopping-distance states.

1.  **Significance**: Quantifies the non-negotiable physical spatial margin that software proposals must clear before motion permission can be granted.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike static geometric obstacle clearance in classical kinematics, dynamic stopping distance grows quadratically with speed ($v^2$), so doubling velocity quadruples the braking term whatever the controller loop rate.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Assuming an emergency stop command halts the machine instantaneously, ignoring that moving mass carries kinetic energy ($E_k = \frac{1}{2}m v^2$) that requires finite mechanical work and braking distance to dissipate.

:::

::: {#fig-02-stopping-distance fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Stopping distance of the warehouse mobile manipulator**: Each bar splits the stop into blind travel during the pre-brake delay, braking travel under the credible deceleration, and the fixed overhead of the localization bound and protective clearance, against the `{python} BodyStoppingBudget.d_clear_str` rack-end clear distance. Case 1 counts only the terms the body owns at the `{python} BodyStoppingBudget.v_str` drive limit and stops within `{python} BodyStoppingBudget.case_body_str`. Case 2 adds the full `{python} BodyStoppingBudget.tau_full_str` pre-brake delay that later chapters assemble, the lease path of @sec-nervous-cadences plus the observation age of @sec-perception; at `{python} BodyStoppingBudget.case_full_str` it still fits, although later chapters add a stop profile and a tracking bound. Case 3 raises speed to a hypothetical `{python} BodyStoppingBudget.v_fast_str`, above the drive limit, with the same delay; braking travel grows by `{python} BodyStoppingBudget.brake_growth_pct_str` and the stop, at `{python} BodyStoppingBudget.case_fast_str`, breaches the clear distance." fig-alt="Horizontal stacked bars for three cases, each split into blind travel, braking travel, and fixed overhead, against a dashed vertical line marking the rack-end clear distance. The first two bars end inside the line with the remaining margin shaded green; the third bar extends past the line into a hatched red breach."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ STOPPING DISTANCE OF THE RUNNING MACHINE (FIGURE)
# │ Context: @fig-02-stopping-distance
# │ Goal:    show why velocity, not latency, dominates the defended clearance
# │ Show:    the three-term decomposition for the body-only terms, the full
# │          pre-brake delay, and a speed-scaling case, against D_clear
# │ How:     cases from BodyStoppingBudget (calc_safe_stopping_distance with
# │          RM and AISLE); d_stop = v*tau + v^2/(2a) + delta_loc + delta_margin
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import viz

MM = ureg.millimeter

# ┌── 1. LOAD (from the stopping-budget cell) ──────────────────────────────────
S = BodyStoppingBudget  # category: derived (values keep their budget-cell categories)
A_BRAKE = S.a_brake  # category: illustrative (loaded, dry floor)
OVERHEAD = S.overhead.to(MM).magnitude  # category: derived (illustrative delta_loc plus chosen delta_margin)
D_CLEAR = S.d_clear.to(MM).magnitude  # category: illustrative (rack-end clear distance)
CASES = [  # category: illustrative and derived (drive-limit and speed-scaling cases from the budget cell)
    ("Case 1", "Partial budget:\nbody terms only", S.v, S.t_act),
    ("Case 2", "Full delay", S.v, S.tau_full),
    ("Case 3", "Full delay, faster", S.v_fast, S.tau_full),
]

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
rows = []
for name, sub, v, tau in CASES:
    react = (v * tau).to(MM).magnitude
    brake = (v**2 / (2 * A_BRAKE)).to(MM).magnitude
    rows.append((name, sub, react, brake, react + brake + OVERHEAD))

# ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
check(abs(rows[0][4] - S.case_body.magnitude) < 1e-6, "Case 1 must match the budget cell.")
check(abs(rows[1][4] - S.case_full.magnitude) < 1e-6, "Case 2 must match the budget cell.")
check(abs(rows[2][4] - S.case_fast.magnitude) < 1e-6, "Case 3 must match the budget cell.")

# ┌── 4. PLOT ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig, ax, COLORS, plt = viz.setup_plot(figsize=(9, 3.6))
H = 0.58
for i, (name, sub, react, brake, stop) in enumerate(rows):
    y = len(rows) - 1 - i
    left = 0.0
    for width, color, label in (
        (react, COLORS["BlueL"], "Blind travel"),
        (brake, COLORS["BlueLine"], "Braking"),
        (OVERHEAD, COLORS["grid"], "Overhead"),
    ):
        ax.barh(y, width, left=left, height=H, color=color, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.8, label=label if i == 0 else None, zorder=3)
        left += width
    if stop <= D_CLEAR:
        ax.barh(
            y,
            D_CLEAR - stop,
            left=stop,
            height=H,
            color=COLORS["GreenFill"],
            edgecolor="white",
            linewidth=0.8,
            label="Remaining margin" if i == 0 else None,
            zorder=3,
        )
    else:
        ax.barh(
            y,
            stop - D_CLEAR,
            left=D_CLEAR,
            height=H,
            facecolor="none",
            edgecolor=COLORS["RedLine"],
            linewidth=1.0,
            hatch="//",
            label="Breach" if i == len(rows) - 1 else None,
            zorder=4,
        )
    ax.text(-25, y, f"{name}\n{sub}", ha="right", va="center", fontsize=9, linespacing=1.4)
    ax.text(max(stop, D_CLEAR) + 25, y, f"{stop:,.1f} mm", va="center", fontsize=8.5, color=COLORS["primary"], zorder=6)

ax.axvline(D_CLEAR, color=COLORS["RedLine"], lw=1.4, linestyle=(0, (5, 4)), zorder=5)
ax.text(D_CLEAR, len(rows) - 0.42, f"  rack end at {S.d_clear.to(ureg.meter).magnitude:.2f} m", color=COLORS["RedLine"], fontsize=9, va="bottom")

ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_xlim(0, 1700)
ax.set_ylim(-0.7, len(rows) - 0.25)
ax.set_xlabel("Distance traveled before rest (mm)")
ax.grid(True, axis="x", zorder=0)
ax.grid(False, axis="y")
for side in ("left", "top", "right"):
    ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
handles, labels = ax.get_legend_handles_labels()
seen = dict(zip(labels, handles))
ax.legend(seen.values(), seen.keys(), loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.22), ncol=5, frameon=False, fontsize=8.5)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

:::

### Dynamic velocity ceilings and clearance budgeting {#sec-body-dynamic-velocity-ceilings}

The bars in @fig-02-stopping-distance separate two design changes. Adding delay at the drive limit consumes part of the remaining clearance; increasing speed also enlarges the braking term quadratically. All three cases are illustrative calculations under the same constant-deceleration model. The first isolates the body's contribution, the second includes a selected end-to-end delay, and the third tests a hypothetical speed above the drive limit. Their comparison motivates a speed ceiling that changes with available clearance, rather than a fixed speed limit independent of the scene.

For a stationary obstacle detected at distance $D_{\text{clear}}$, such as a person standing at the rack end or a dropped tote, the modeled stopping distance must fit the clear path, $d_{\text{stop}} \le D_{\text{clear}}$. This is the condition that principle \ref{pri-vol4-irreversibility} places on every stop, now with each term of $d_{\text{stop}}$ a limit of this machine. With conservative timing and braking bounds, the permission path can solve this inequality for a ceiling on new velocity proposals $v_{\text{max}}$. The positive root of the quadratic inequality[^fn-math-velocity-root] is:
$$v_{\text{max}} = -a_{\text{brake}} \tau_{\text{delay}} + \sqrt{(a_{\text{brake}} \tau_{\text{delay}})^2 + 2 a_{\text{brake}} (D_{\text{clear}} - \delta_{\text{loc}} - \delta_{\text{margin}})}$$
When sensor range degrades or an obstacle enters the trajectory, $D_{\text{clear}}$ contracts and lowers the ceiling, provided the available distance remains nonnegative. At zero available distance the ceiling is zero. If the machine is already moving, however, a zero setpoint cannot remove its current stopping distance; a negative available distance means the admission condition is already violated and requires an emergency response.

[^fn-math-velocity-root]: **Kinematic Velocity Root**\index{Kinematic velocity root!quadratic clearance}: Grouping the constant spatial terms into available physical distance $D_{\text{avail}} = D_{\text{clear}} - \delta_{\text{loc}} - \delta_{\text{margin}}$ yields the quadratic inequality $\frac{1}{2 a_{\text{brake}}} v^2 + \tau_{\text{delay}} v - D_{\text{avail}} \le 0$. Multiplying by $2 a_{\text{brake}}$ produces $v^2 + 2 a_{\text{brake}} \tau_{\text{delay}} v - 2 a_{\text{brake}} D_{\text{avail}} \le 0$. Applying the quadratic formula and taking the positive physical root defines the dynamic velocity ceiling.

::: {#nbk-body-stopping-distance-budgeting-high-tail-compute .callout-notebook title="The body's stopping distance"}
**Problem**: The warehouse mobile manipulator, loaded to at most `{python} MachineMomentum.m_loaded_str`, drives toward a rack end at its $v =$ `{python} BodyStoppingBudget.v_str` drive limit, and a person stands in the aisle at the clear distance $D_{\text{clear}} =$ `{python} BodyStoppingBudget.d_clear_str`. The body owns three terms of @eq-body-stopping-distance: braking travel under the credible deceleration $a_{\text{brake}} =$ `{python} BodyStoppingBudget.a_brake_str` (loaded, dry floor); the fixed overhead of the localization bound $\delta_{\text{loc}} =$ `{python} BodyStoppingBudget.delta_loc_str` and the protective clearance $\delta_{\text{margin}} =$ `{python} BodyStoppingBudget.delta_margin_str`; and the brake onset $T_{\text{act}} =$ `{python} BodyStoppingBudget.t_act_str`, which enters $\tau_{\text{delay}}$. How much of the clear distance do these terms use, what speed would they alone permit, and how do speed and added delay change the answer?

**1. Braking travel:**
For the same credible deceleration, mass cancels from the work-energy balance. The loaded machine's `{python} MachineMomentum.e_k_str` sets the energy the stopping system must absorb or dissipate, while the specified deceleration sets the braking distance. A different payload can change that deceleration and requires a new bound:
`{python} BodyStoppingBudget.d_brake_display_math`
The stopping distance so far is `{python} BodyStoppingBudget.d_brake_str`.

**2. Fixed overhead:**
`{python} BodyStoppingBudget.overhead_display_math`
The running total rises to `{python} BodyStoppingBudget.total_2_str`.

**3. Brake onset:**
Between the brake command and the first retarding force, the base still moves at full speed:
`{python} BodyStoppingBudget.d_onset_display_math`
`{python} BodyStoppingBudget.total_display_math`
The body's own terms leave `{python} BodyStoppingBudget.remaining_str` of the `{python} BodyStoppingBudget.d_clear_str` clear distance for every delay the body does not own.

**4. The body-only ceiling:**
Solving @eq-body-stopping-distance for speed with $\tau_{\text{delay}} = T_{\text{act}}$:
`{python} BodyStoppingBudget.ceiling_display_math`
The body alone would permit `{python} BodyStoppingBudget.v_ceiling_str`, above the drive limit. @Sec-nervous and @sec-perception add the delay terms that spend part of this headroom.

**5. Speed against delay:**
At a hypothetical `{python} BodyStoppingBudget.v_fast_str`, above the drive limit, the braking term alone grows to `{python} BodyStoppingBudget.d_brake_fast_str`, `{python} BodyStoppingBudget.brake_growth_pct_str` more than at the drive limit. At the drive limit, each additional `{python} BodyStoppingBudget.dt_extra_str` of pre-brake delay adds `{python} BodyStoppingBudget.d_per_extra_str`.

**Architect's Rule of Thumb**: *Never raise a velocity setpoint without re-solving the clearance quadratic.*
:::

### Applying the velocity ceiling {#sec-body-velocity-governor-cbf}

A speed ceiling becomes useful when the permission path checks it before accepting each new velocity request. The learned policy proposes a speed; the independent check uses clearance, delay, and available deceleration to decide whether that request fits the stopping budget. A lower requested speed changes future motion, but cannot erase the distance needed to stop from the current speed. The check must therefore examine the current state as well as the candidate command.

The online velocity governor applies this comparison at each control tick. Its modeled feasible set is $\mathcal{C} = \{ (\mathbf{x}, v) : d_{\text{stop}}(v) \le D_{\text{clear}} \}$: the combinations of position and speed for which stopping fits the available clearance under the declared assumptions. Example \ref{exmp-body-dynamic-velocity-ceiling-governor-1-khz} checks current feasibility and clamps a new request to the computed ceiling. Keeping the real machine within that set between checks also requires bounds on timing, obstacle motion, and actuator response; the calculation alone does not establish those bounds.

::: {#exmp-body-dynamic-velocity-ceiling-governor-1-khz .callout-example title="Dynamic velocity ceiling governor"}
**Inputs**:

- $D_{\text{clear}} \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$: Detected obstacle distance along travel vector $[\text{m}]$.
- $\tau_{\text{delay}} \in \mathbb{R}_{> 0}$: Conservatively bounded sense-to-braking delay, including actuator response $[\text{s}]$.
- $a_{\text{brake}} \in \mathbb{R}_{> 0}$: Conservative lower bound on available brake deceleration under the declared load and surface $[\text{m/s}^2]$.
- $\delta_{\text{loc}}, \delta_{\text{margin}} \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$: Localization uncertainty bound and physical clearance margin $[\text{m}]$.
- $v_{\text{now}} \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$: Current forward speed $[\text{m/s}]$.
- $v_{\text{cand}} \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$: Candidate forward velocity setpoint proposed by neural policy $[\text{m/s}]$.

**Output**:

- $v_{\text{safe}} \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$: Clamped velocity request within the modeled ceiling $[\text{m/s}]$.

**Admission Check** (while the current state is feasible):

1. Modeled stopping distance: $d_{\text{stop}}(v_{\text{safe}}) = v_{\text{safe}} \tau_{\text{delay}} + \frac{v_{\text{safe}}^2}{2 a_{\text{brake}}} + \delta_{\text{loc}} + \delta_{\text{margin}} \le D_{\text{clear}}$ for a stationary obstacle.
2. Non-Negativity: $v_{\text{safe}} \ge 0.0$.

**Algorithm Steps**:

1. Compute available physical braking distance:
   $$D_{\text{avail}} \leftarrow D_{\text{clear}} - \delta_{\text{loc}} - \delta_{\text{margin}}$$

2. If $D_{\text{avail}} \le 0.0$, no positive travel distance remains within the declared protective margin. Reject the proposal, hold setpoints at zero if stationary, or command the maximum available emergency braking response if moving, and assert the clearance loss flag. Otherwise check $v_{\text{now}}\tau_{\text{delay}} + v_{\text{now}}^2/(2a_{\text{brake}}) \le D_{\text{avail}}$ before admitting another proposal. If that check fails, request the same emergency response and flag lost feasibility. Loss of this modeled margin does not by itself establish an unavoidable collision, and a zero velocity setpoint cannot stop existing motion immediately.
3. Compute quadratic discriminant:
   $$\text{disc} \leftarrow (a_{\text{brake}} \tau_{\text{delay}})^2 + 2 a_{\text{brake}} D_{\text{avail}}$$

4. Solve positive physical root for dynamic velocity ceiling:
   $$v_{\max} \leftarrow -a_{\text{brake}} \tau_{\text{delay}} + \sqrt{\text{disc}}$$

5. Enforce dynamic clamping against policy proposal:
   $$v_{\text{safe}} \leftarrow \min(v_{\text{cand}}, \max(0.0, v_{\max}))$$

6. Return $v_{\text{safe}}$.
:::

The quadratic turns a fixed speed limit into a clearance-dependent ceiling for new proposals. If perception range degrades, sensor latency spikes, or braking friction drops, the permission path must reduce admitted speed before clearance is exhausted or execute a defined risk-reducing fallback. Preserving a feasible set through continuing motion requires a dynamic admission rule; @sec-enforcement develops control barrier functions [@ames2019control] for that purpose. Here the result is a one-dimensional stopping-feasibility check whose assumptions remain explicit.

Enforcing this speed limit assumes the permission path can demand the deceleration $a_{\text{brake}}$ whenever safety requires it. Yet commanding rapid deceleration requires sudden, large mechanical torque from the drive motors and gearboxes. If the permission path requests a torque step that exceeds what the actuator bandwidth budget allows, the mechanical body cannot deliver the required deceleration, invalidating the model-based stopping ceiling and risking collision. The same drives also shape what happens if the stop falls short. The reflected rotor energy counted in $m_{\text{eff}}$ then reaches the obstacle and the gear teeth through the transmission's compliance, so the stopping calculation cannot substitute for a contact-load assessment.

## Actuator Transmission Limits {#sec-body-actuator-limits}
